#4758. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Your hub for heart health management, insights, and solutions

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This new study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

This was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

The researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

They measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

The researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

Among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

When the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is important to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

These findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” said Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

“Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd said.

Judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more important to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

She said that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is important to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

“I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” said Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”

#4757. Does Black Friday Make Everything Else Seem Expensive?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

There is something rather irritating about seeing a product heavily discounted during the Black Friday sales, only to see it back at full price a few days later. Before the sale, the original price might have seemed perfectly reasonable. But once the excitement of the sale has died down, it feels expensive, and paying the full price seems almost painful.

Black Friday discounts might do more than encourage us to spend money during the sales. They could also change our perception of value and how much we're willing to pay for things long after the bargains have disappeared.

When we buy something, we tend to think that we're making a rational judgment about whether it's worth the price. But how do we decide what something is actually worth?

One way is by comparing the asking price with what we've paid before or what we've seen the product selling for elsewhere. This gives us what is known as a reference price, a sort of benchmark we use to decide whether something seems expensive or cheap.

Over time, and after many repeated purchases, we become accustomed to paying a certain amount for a particular product. We accept that amount as its normal price, and it becomes what we expect to pay. But then Black Friday happens, which nowadays may last for a full month rather than one day, and that same product is suddenly available for considerably less.

Even though we know perfectly well that the discount is temporary, that lower price starts to influence what we think the product should cost. It can become a new reference point against which we judge future prices.

When the sale ends and the price returns to normal, the amount we have become used to paying no longer seems quite so reasonable. The deal has changed our perception of value.

When a discount changes what we think something is worth, it can also change whether we're willing to buy it at all.

Across three studies, Guo (2026) found that consumers who had seen an extremely low price were less willing to buy the same product later at a higher price than those who had seen a smaller discount. What was interesting was why they didn't want to buy it.

Seeing the lower price reduced how much participants thought the product was worth. The prospect of paying the higher price also increased their anticipated regret. They expected to feel worse about buying something they knew had previously been priced for considerably less.

It didn't matter whether participants had previously bought the product at the cheaper price. Simply knowing it had once been available for less was enough to discourage a future purchase. We don't necessarily have to miss out on a bargain for it to change our perception of value, which the researcher called the postdiscount effect.

The findings raise an interesting question about Black Friday. If retailers spend weeks convincing us that their products are worth buying at heavily discounted prices, what happens when they expect us to start paying full price again?

This is where Black Friday might become a problem for retailers themselves. Black Friday is designed to encourage us to buy more by making products temporarily cheaper. But in doing so, retailers may also be changing what we're willing to pay for those products in the future. They could be inadvertently teaching us that their products are worth less than they originally claimed.

The more accustomed we become to seeing discounts, the more we might begin questioning whether the full price is ever worth paying. Why buy something today when it might be cheaper again next month in the post-Christmas sales? Why pay the normal price when we've seen exactly how little a retailer was prepared to sell it for last week?

There's nothing wrong with taking advantage of a good Black Friday discount. You've made a sensible decision if you've been planning to buy something and find it cheaper. The problem is when we allow that temporary price to determine what we think something should cost long after the sales have finished.

That's the irony of Black Friday. Retailers spend much of November getting us excited and convincing us that we're going to get extraordinary value for our money. In doing so, they might also be convincing us that their products were never worth the original asking price.

They may have saved us money today, but they've made everything seem more expensive tomorrow.

Guo, T. (2026). From inaction inertia to the postdiscount effect: How a lower price reduces subsequent purchase after it expires. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 39(4), e70092

#4755. A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” said study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The new review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

Laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

“Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep issues related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

“A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein said. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein said.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

“For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein said. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”

Sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

“I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein said. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”

#4754. Zines Are a Great Tool for Learning

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

A zine (pronounced “zeen”) is a little booklet or mini-magazine you make yourself, combining elements of a scrapbook, journal, collage, or a handmade book. You can write, draw, add photos, stickers, quotes, stories, or anything else you want to express. Everything is customizable, from page size and arrangement to colors, materials, and overall look and feel. Zines have a long history of giving people excluded from mainstream publishing a way to share their ideas, experiences, art, and perspectives. Today, zine-making is a worldwide culture, with makers sharing and trading their work at fairs, festivals, libraries, bookstores, and community spaces. The zine has become a cultural icon with a distinct history, community, and spirit of creative independence.

Zine-making is a form of project-based learning and a student-centered way of learning through creating something meaningful. Project-based learning gives people an active role: they explore questions, solve problems, make choices, connect ideas, and apply what they are learning to real situations. Zines bring some especially useful qualities to that process. They give people many ways to work with an idea through writing, images, collage, humor, stories, symbols, personal experience, or cultural references, while also asking them to think about who will read or see the zine and how they want to communicate with that audience. The finished zine becomes something they can hold, share, discuss, and return to later. Across studies in classrooms and museums, zine-making has helped people connect course or exhibit content with their own experiences and interests, while giving them space to shape that learning into something distinctly their own.

Psychologically, making a zine brings together what a person notices, remembers, feels, experiences, questions, and connects while they are actively making something. As they revisit what they know, new information connects with prior experience and can reshape how they understand it. Putting ideas into words, images, and materials makes those ideas visible, giving the person something to reconsider and change. Thinking about an audience shapes how they communicate, while reflection can also turn inward toward identity and belief. Through this process, people build knowledge that feels meaningful and personal.

In this zine, the maker transforms a museum visit into a reflection on love, connection, memory, and being alive. Using photographs from the visit, handwritten thoughts, museum materials, collage, thread, and a three-dimensional heart labeled “my core,” they connect dinosaurs, animals, ancient history, memory, and emotion through themes of love and interconnectedness. Museum content becomes part of a personal interpretation, helping the maker explore what the visit means to them and communicate that meaning to others.

In this zine, a student transforms educational psychology concepts into a personal explanation of learning. They use gears to represent thinking, a bell for behavior and conditioning, drawings of memory and motivation, and a child connecting ideas across the page. They also develop their own argument that creativity is a form of intelligence, extending the course material with a personal claim. By choosing how to connect and visually represent these concepts, the student creates both a reflection on their learning and an expression of how they understand education.

Zine-making is accessible almost anywhere, from homes and classrooms to museums and community spaces, using simple materials like paper, pens, magazines, photos, and stickers.

Anyone can make a zine, so give it a try and see what emerges!

April Ursula Fox, Ph.D. (UNLV), is an educational psychology teacher and researcher whose work explores learner agency, multimodal learning, and applied educational psychology across formal and informal learning environments.

Your nutrient needs change as you age—here’s how to fill in the gaps.

Even if you pride yourself on eating whole foods and cooking healthy meals, it can still be super hard to get all of the vitamins and minerals your body needs. Plus, your nutrient needs change as you age.

For instance, “as women navigate through the wonderful world of the menopause transition, there are changes, health-wise, that happen,” says Leslie Bonci, RD, a sports dietitian based in Pittsburgh. As your hormone levels start to decrease, you may be more likely to lose bone density and muscle mass. When these changes happen, “there are certain nutrients that are going to be needed more than others,” she adds. That’s when it can be helpful to turn to a supplement.

Meet the experts: Leslie Bonci, RD, is a sports dietitian based in Pittsburgh. Navya Mysore, MD, is a primary care physician, women's health expert, and WH advisory board member based in New York City.

Knowing which supplements you should take in each stage of life may be complicated, but we found the right experts to simplify everything. Consider this your supplement roadmap.

First, have a conversation with your primary care physician—they should know about all of the medications and supplements you’re currently taking or are considering. Your doc will help you ensure supplementation is the best course of action after considering your holistic health care plan. Then, they can rule out any potential medication interactions and decide which dosage is best, says Navya Mysore, MD, a primary care physician, women's health expert, and WH advisory board member based in New York City.

Here are some of the most common interactions, per Dr. Mysore and Bonci:

You also might want to get blood work done before starting a supplement, especially if you think you may have a deficiency. “Checking things like iron stores (ferritin), vitamin D, or B12 can tell you if you actually need a supplement and how much,” says Dr. Mysore. However, you don’t need blood work if you’re just taking a basic prenatal or multivitamin.

Just remember: “Supplements are a complement to—not a replacement for—eating,” Bonci says. They’re just one piece of the puzzle; in order to live your healthiest, longest, best life, you’ll want to make sure you’re eating nutritiously and exercising consistently.

Sorry to our gummy lovers out there: “Capsules usually win—they tend to absorb better and have fewer fillers,” says Dr. Mysore. “Tablets are fine but a bit more variable.” Unfortunately, gummies are often underdosed and may not include key nutrients like iron, she adds. So, your safest bet is a capsule.

#4751. ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

These expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include new clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep issues, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

“This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these issues.

According to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies showed some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

It also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:

Research shows that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

“This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” said Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

Currently, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

There are currently two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

There are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

“Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document shows what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” said Pier.

When I teach positive psychology, a topic students are interested in is “What makes us happy?” What actions can we take to increase our experience of psychological well-being? With Black Friday here and many of us buying things we want or need, you can make smarter purchases for greater joy in life.

I’ll start with the bottom line: Research consistently shows that experiences make us much happier (and for longer) than material items (TV, sofa, a gadget).

5. Chan and Mogilner (2016) ran four studies and found that experiential gifts strengthen the bond between giver and recipient more than material ones. The reason is emotional evocativeness: an experience triggers strong feelings when you recall it (remember that special vacation?) while the sofa won’t. It’s all about meaning.

When you are contemplating your next Black Friday purchases, consider these studies. Many other studies point the same way. Ask yourself what you really want from your purchases, and invest in the ones that bring you more happiness, meaning, and connection with yourself and others.

Chan, C., & Mogilner, C. (2017). Experiential gifts foster stronger social relationships than material gifts. Journal of Consumer Research, 43(6), 913–931. https://doi.org/10.1093/jcr/ucw067

Kumar, A., Killingsworth, M. A., & Gilovich, T. (2014). Waiting for Merlot: Anticipatory consumption of experiential and material purchases. Psychological Science, 25(10), 1924–1931. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797614546556

Van Boven, L., Campbell, M. C., & Gilovich, T. (2010). Stigmatizing materialism: On stereotypes and impressions of materialistic and experiential pursuits. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 36(4), 551–563. https://doi.org/10.1177/0146167210362790

Van Boven, L., & Gilovich, T. (2003). To do or to have? That is the question. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 85(6), 1193–1202. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.85.6.1193

#4748. Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

While MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” said Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

New diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder said.

“Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also important to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as new evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

“MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder said.

“For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

“MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder said. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several important changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include new MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

If you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder said.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is important that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”

Allder said that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

“A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder said.

#4747. How to Maneuver Generational Differences Over the Holidays

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

With the holidays yet again upon us, people will be setting their holiday gathering plans and preparing for an onslaught of multi-generational togetherness. When coming together for the holidays, the goal isn’t necessarily for everyone to think or celebrate alike; it’s to celebrate harmony and happiness while making room for the differences that you know may come with getting so many people of varying ages together in one room.

Here, we discuss how to make room at one’s table for generational differences while protecting the deep thread of connection that makes everyone family.

We’ve all experienced it. The sideways glances at the child who won’t eat their turkey. The sighs and stories about “Back in my day…” The admonishment to the teenager to “put your phone away.” The mom in the middle of it all who just wants a group photo of everyone before they dig in.

These are the sights and sounds of most holiday family gatherings. The younger generation has taken over the planning and organization of events, while the older generation sits in the wake of it all, wondering why anything had to change.

Even though the holidays bring together people who love one another, they can also bring friction. According to a 2023 American Psychological Association poll, 89% of U.S. adults reported holiday-related stress, and 22% identified the experience or anticipation of family conflict as a source of that stress.

However, generational differences don’t have to derail a holiday gathering. Once we learn to stop anticipating conflict and start remembering the reason we get together in the first place, we can begin looking forward to the fun stories, skill sharing, and memory-making that make the holidays so special.

It can be easy to get immediately annoyed when Grandpa starts talking about how they used to discipline kids or Great Aunt Margaret says that your stuffing was made incorrectly. Try to reframe statements before irritation or misunderstandings get out of control.

For example, instead of getting bothered when an older member of the family admonishes a child for being on their device, think about why they may be mentioning it. Perhaps they want to spend more time talking with the child, or maybe there are some cultural expectations around the holidays at play.

Researchers found that interactions and education can reduce or even eliminate ageism, which can be at play during multi-generational events. By teaching the younger generation about aging and helping them connect with older people, you can eliminate miscommunication, fear, and negative feelings.

Laying out expectations and boundaries can also be an effective way to help the holiday get-together go more smoothly between the generations. Prior to the event, invite the older generations into a conversation about plans. This way, there will be less chance of surprise or disappointment, and the older generation family members will feel like they are contributing.

Take care to ask about meaningful traditions in the family and choose a few to carry on while leaving room for something new. Discuss important topics like gift budgets, transportation, locations, and food options before the holidays so that there is less room for conflict.

Boundaries can sometimes sound like a dirty word to older generations, but they can still be important for intergenerational harmony during the holidays. First, distinguish between what you are willing to compromise on to keep the peace and a personal boundary that absolutely must be respected.

For example, letting Grandma tell stories about her childhood on the farm may not necessarily hurt anyone, but comments about your body, children declining a hug from a relative, or politics may be in need of some boundary-setting intervention. If boundaries that are important to you are repeatedly ignored, have a place you can go to take a break or a code word with your partner to signal that you need some help getting out of a conversation.

When you get different generations of family together for the holiday, there is bound to be some friction. We live in increasingly divided times, and people may feel more comfortable around their family letting conflicting opinions fly. Holiday hosts should aim to connect the generations instead of steeling themselves for inevitable discourse.

The ultimate goal isn’t to resolve all differences and agree every step of the way (that’s likely impossible). Instead, families should make room for stories, laughter, and the kind of connection that’s only possible between people who know one another as well as family members do.

1. “Even a joyous holiday season can cause stress for most Americans”. (2023, November 30). American Psychological Association. Retrieved November 2, 2026, from https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2023/11/holiday-season-stress.

2. Burnes, D., Sheppard, C., Henderson, C. R., Wassel, M., Cope, R., Barber, C., & Pillemer, K. (2019). Interventions to reduce ageism against older adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis. American Journal of Public Health, 109(8). https://doi.org/10.2105/ajph.2019.305123

#4746. 16 Best Strength Training Exercises to Build Muscle and Strength Fast

There’s no shortage of strength training exercises to pepper into your muscle-building routine. If you’re a regular on FitTok, you might’ve noticed that a new exercise seems to pop up regularly. So, which ones should you pepper into your routine?

“It all comes down to your goal,” says Angela Gargano, a trainer and creator of Strong Feels Good & Pull-up Revolution. The exercises you fill your program with are your most important tools for success.

Keep reading for the best strength training exercises to try, exactly how to add them into a total-body routine, and expert-backed tips for making a plan that works. Ready to get lifting?

Build lasting strength with the WH+ Strong Over 50 Plan, here

Below, we’ve rounded up some of our favorite strength training exercises, spanning all the different muscle groups. Here’s how to create a well-rounded full-body routine you can do regularly.

Equipment: Dumbbells, kettlebell, resistance band | Good for: Total body Instructions: Pick one move from each category—push, pull, hinge, lunge, squat—to create a total body workout. Do it two to three days a week, preferably on nonconsecutive days. For each move, do the allocated amount of sets and reps, resting for 1 to 2 minutes between sets. Select weights that make the last few reps challenging, but doable (and more on selecting weights, below!).

Alternatively, you can split up muscle groups if you have multiple days a week to work out (if you’re working out only two days a week or less, stick with a full-body plan). There are a few ways to do this. If you're planning on strength training twice a week, you can also opt to do one upper-body day (the push/pull exercises) and one lower-body day (the hinge/lunge/squat exercises). Select four or five exercises with a variety of exercise type (don’t fill a lower body day with only squats, no matter how much you love them!) to create your workout.

Or, if you're working out three times a week, you can split your workouts to do one push/pull day, and two hinge/lunge/squat days, or vice versa, depending on what part of your body you want to strengthen most. If you're training more than three times a week, you can split by muscle group.

Here are 16 of the best strength training exercises to fill in your workout.

Why it rocks: Pushups are a classic move for a reason: They work your chest, shoulders, and triceps. Another perk? They engage your core muscles and build functional strength.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 or 4 sets of 8 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: Unlike a standard shoulder press, this upper-body exercise challenges all three muscle heads of your deltoids.

Why it rocks: This is an excellent bent-over row variation that targets your lats and rhomboids, requiring less core stability than a traditional bent-over row.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: Deadlifts build overall strength and power in the posterior chain muscles, including the hamstrings, glutes, and lower back.

Strength training can help you build and maintain muscle mass, improve your joint and bone health, support better body composition, and even increase your longevity. And, including it in your routine is easy to do, as long as you follow these tips and tricks.

“The biggest thing in putting together your entire workout is making sure that you have a proper warm-up, always, no matter what,” says Gargano. “People tend to throw that out the window but dynamic moves are going to help you wake the body up a little bit before you get into your strength training.”

To execute a proper warm-up, select 3 to 4 dynamic and mobility exercises (these are a few of our favorites!) and do them for 30 seconds apiece, 2 or 3 times through. If you're planning on exercising a specific part of your body that day, make sure your warm-up is tailored to that (e.g., if you're about to do a leg day lift, select a few warm-up moves that promote blood flow to the lower body, like lateral lunges or the World's Greatest Stretch).

“In your programming, there’s a combination of things you should always have,” says Gargano, noting you don’t have to put them all in the same workout/day, but they should certainly all fit in your week: Push movements (like pushups and chest presses), pull movements (like pull-ups and rows), squats, lunges, and hinge movements (think: deadlifts, hip hinges).

Programming your workouts will largely depend on how many times a week you work out (more on that here). The more times a week you can exercise, the more you can split your workouts by muscle group. For example, if you're working out three days per week, you might be interested in doing one upper-body day, one leg day focused on glutes and hamstrings, and another focused on quads and calves. If you're only working out twice per week, you'll want to make sure you're programming for the whole body: at least one upper-body lift and one lower-body lift.

“I know people are going to be like, ‘Well, what about my core?’ but your core is used in all those movements,” Gargano assures.

“You want to be sure that you're working all the body parts so that you're not uneven,” says Gargano. It's an issue trainers see a lot—people focus so hard on defining one part of their body that they neglect the rest. For example, if you're aiming to build up your glutes, don't only do hip thrusts on lower body day. Incorporate some lunges and squats in there, too, to strengthen your quad muscles so they can work in tandem with your strong glutes.

As long as you hit all five of the main movement patterns we named earlier (push, pull, squat, lunge, hip hinge) throughout the week, you should be in good shape.

A few weeks into your workout program, your body will get used to what you’re doing—so you'll need to level up the challenge, “so that your body can continue to develop and work the muscles in different ways,” says Gargano. That means increasing your weights, reps, or sets to progressively overload the muscles—doing so will help them get continuously stronger, and ensure your performance never plateaus.

To know when to up the weights, use the two-for-two rule: Once you can do two extra good-form reps beyond your planned rep target for two workouts in a row, you’re ready to increase your load. From there, try to increase 2.5 to 5 pounds for upper-body exercises, and 5 to 10 pounds for lower-body exercises. But remember, this is just a recommendation—you can do more or less based on how you specifically feel.

The best exercise plan is the one you're going to stick to. And the one you're going to stick to is the one that best fits into your schedule.

“You need to figure out what is working well for you and your body,” says Gargano. “Everybody's different, so try out two days a week first, and then if you feel good, maybe add that third day.”

Once you have your schedule set, don't feel like it's an end-all, be-all. The more you can hit your workouts, the better—but there's no reason to knock yourself down if things get busy and you miss one or two. You can always abbreviate your workout by cutting a few exercises or sets, or get moving by going for a brief walk. The key is to stay moving as much as you can. It won't always be perfect, and that's okay.

#4745. Lifting Heavy Isn’t the Whole Story When It Comes to Building Strength. Here's What to Do Instead.

My name is Cori Ritchey, and I am an exercise physiology nerd turned fitness journalist, and the fitness editor at Women’s Health. When I’m not writing, editing, and researching fitness, I’m teaching it to my personal training and group fitness clients. In my new column, Between Sets, I’m pulling back the curtain on the same advice, tips, and ‘aha!’ moments I share with my clients while they’re catching their breath. Stick around for the strategic, science-backed nuggets that’ll help you move better, train smarter, and actually enjoy the process.

Scroll any fitness feed and you’ll see it: people clanging plates, chasing PRs, and even pulling dangerous stunts for the pride of lifting heavy. And where there’s real joy in getting stronger, there’s also real pressure to keep adding weight.

As a strength and conditioning coach and the fitness editor at Women’s Health, I’ve been preaching the lift-heavy-or-go-home gospel for years. For valid reason: challenging your muscles over time is one of the most reliable ways to build lasting strength, support bone health, improve body composition, and stay functional as we age.

The “lift heavy” ethos isn’t new. Strength training is as old as Ancient Greece, where the first gyms were developed. It progressed through decades of physical culture into Muscle Beach, USA, the birthplace of American lifting that started as a beachside gymnastics park in Venice Beach, California, in the 1940s. It was there, too, where the first American women bodybuilders, like legendary Abbey Stockton, emerged—at a time when many scientists still believed lifting was bad for the body.

Research eventually caught up to what lifters were already experiencing: resistance training works. More women, especially in recent years, started showing up for it, too. In 2004, 17 percent of women reported regularly participating in weight lifting. By 2020, that number has bumped to nearly 30 percent. Then came the influencer era, amplifying a message that’s equal parts motivating and misleading: lifting weights is good for you—but it has to be heavy to count.

There’s a kernel of truth in there. Progressive overload (the process of gradually increasing the stress you put on your body in a workout) builds muscle and strength, and increasing load is an efficient way to do so.

And that matters—especially when heavier, heavier, heavier simply isn’t in the cards.

Because for many, it’s not. It requires access to specific equipment, time to train consistently without rushing through sets, and quality coaching and information to nail form and stay injury-free. It also has to be safe and appropriate for your body on any given day—whether you’re navigating chronic illness, postpartum or perimenopause realities, and injury history, or limiting pain. And even when everything lines up on paper, there’s a very real mental hurdle: walking into a gym and loading up a bar can be intimidating as hell.

Still, if you’re here to build strength, change your body composition, protect your bone health, or invest in your movement longevity, lifting heavier will certainly help—but it’s not the only path to lifelong strength. Somewhere along the way, “heavy” became synonymous with “effective”, and “light” or "moderate" became codes for “waste of time.”

The exercise research world is finding that’s not the case. “You don't need to do anything heavy for the health benefits of resistance exercise to take place,” says Stuart Phillips, PhD, kinesiology professor and hypertrophy researcher at McMaster University.

Adequate research has suggested that hypertrophy (the fancy scientific term for muscle growth) is not determined by a magic rep goal or the weight on the bar, says Susie Reiner, PhD, CSCS, is an exercise physiologist, assistant professor of exercise science at Seton Hall University, and CEO of TheoryEx, a sport science research and consulting firm. “Instead, hypertrophy appears to be driven by whether a training set provides a sufficiently strong internal stimulus to the muscle, which is reasonably defined as effort and proximity to muscular failure.”

Trainers have traditionally been taught that specific rep ranges map neatly to specific goals: 1 to 3 for power, 3 to 8 for strength, 8 to 12 for muscle, and 12-plus for muscular endurance. But newer findings show you can build muscle across a much wider rep range—roughly as low as 5 and as high as 25, Phillips says. “There is, then, by definition, no sweet spot for muscle building, because the whole repetition range then becomes the sweet spot.”

Across several studies and meta-analyses, similar muscle growth has been seen between people who train with lighter loads (about 30 to 40 percent of their one-rep maximum), and those who train with heavier loads (about 70 to 85 percent of their one-rep maximum)—as long as sets are taken close enough to failure.

Muscle growth is dependent on recruiting and fatiguing a large portion of muscle fibers, Reiner says. Your muscles need a reason to adapt. With heavier weights for fewer reps, you recruit a lot of fibers immediately. With lighter weights for higher reps, you recruit them more gradually.

One thing to note here: while a large percentage of these studies have only been done in men, Phillips notes that “the work that has been done in women shows us that actually men and women respond very, very similarly to weight lifting in terms of muscle mass gain. Women have less baseline muscle, but relatively speaking, they gain the same amount as men—that's been robustly shown.” Phillips and his colleagues are currently running several studies (including one study specific to perimenopausal women!) that will further clarify what this looks like in women.

Researchers feel confident that as long as sets are taken sufficiently to failure (more on what that means coming up), different loading strategies can produce similar hypertrophy, Reiner says.

Here’s what that looks like IRL: Let’s say you have biceps curls on your workout plan each week. One week, you pick up the 10-pound dumbbells, and do 3 sets of 12 reps. In the sets, when you approach the end of that rep range, it feels tough—you can maybe grind out 2 more reps max. The next week, you reach for the 15s. You can only hit 6 reps before you feel like your form is faltering, but the effort feels similar—you’ve still got about two reps left before your form breaks down.

The heavier weight might feel more empowering, but both workouts deliver a similar muscle-building stimulus—assuming you’re training regularly enough, eating enough protein and calories, and adequately recovering, of course.

Sure, research confirms you don’t have to lift crazy heavy—but that doesn’t mean that coming close to failure feels easy. Failing a rep can be scary (and honestly, discouraging). Here’s the good news: you don’t need true, all-out failure. You just need to train to proximity to failure.

One practical way to gauge that is with the rate of perceived exertion scale. “Rate of perceived exertion (RPE) is a global effort scale, typically ranging from one to 10,” Reiner says. An RPE of 10 represents maximal effort—no chance you could do one more rep. A RPE of nine suggests you could do one more, an RPE of eight means you could probably do two more reps, and so on and so forth.

Muscle growth still occurs between RPE of 7 to 9, Phillips says. “You don’t need it to be a 10 out of 10 where you’re red-lining and can’t get the bar off your chest.” In other words: you can train hard without routinely hitting the point where things get sketchy.

That matters, because the closer you get to all-out failure, the more your injury risk can creep up—especially if you start twisting, bouncing, and compensating to force a rep you simply don’t have.

The failure you want to flirt with is technical failure, or technical fatigue. “Technical failure means you cannot complete another repetition with good form,” Phillips says—that’s where injury risk rises. Muscular failure (otherwise known as momentary failure) occurs when a muscle is unable to generate enough force to complete another rep, regardless of maximal effort. Picture trying to do one more biceps curl and you quite literally cannot lift your arm and the weight up again—that’s muscular failure..

Aim for technical failure. Pushing yourself too far in an effort to achieve muscular failure could cause your body to overcompensate and push you into a compromising position. The good news, too, is technical failure tends to be very close to muscular failure for most people, Phillips says.

A useful rule of thumb: stop when you have one to two perfect-form reps left in the tank.

Yes, you still need to reach for that RPE of 7 to 9—but there’s more ways to do that than just reaching for the next highest weight. Here are some other elements you can play with to up the challenge:

Frequency. Reaching for heavier weights, you can simply aim to reach for any type of weight more often. That might look like increasing your strength training days from two to three days a week.

Volume. Think of your training volume as the amount of weight total you lift during a given session. Sure, lifting heavier loads is one way to increase your total, but it can also be accomplished by increasing the amount of sets or reps you do.

Rest time. Decreasing the amount of rest you allow yourself gives your muscles less time to recover, wearing them out quicker with lighter loads.

Time under tension. The amount of time your muscles work for matters. Increasing your time under tension, or the amount of time your muscles are working in a lift (for example, lowering a curl for a slow four-count).

That all being said, heavier loads might still take the cake in terms of efficiency. You’ll find yourself increasing your frequency and volume to monotonous levels if you never increase your load.

Back to biceps curls: Say you get comfortable at six reps at 15 lbs. After a few weeks, it no longer starts to feel challenging for you, so you increase it eight. And then 10. And then 12. If you never reach for the intimidating 20 lb dumbbells, you’ll eventually find yourself having to do sets of 30 reps just to feel something. And that can become time consuming. You don’t need extremes all the time—but you do need your training to stay challenging.

“For individuals who are uncomfortable training to very high levels of effort, consistent training at moderate-to-high RPEs combined with sufficient volume and progression can still produce meaningful muscle growth,” Reiner says. “From a long-term perspective, hypertrophy depends less on any single maximal set and more on repeated exposure to challenging, well-managed training over weeks and months.”

Convinced to start pushing closer to failure? Here are a few ways to progress safely.

The two-for-two method is a classic progression strategy used by professional trainers. Once you can do two extra proper-form reps beyond your planned rep target for two workouts in a row, you’re ready to increase your load.

Let's use the biceps curl example just one more time. You’ve been training with the 15s for sets of 8, and now you can hit 10 with clean form for two workouts in a row. That’s your cue to grab 17.5s the next go.

How much should you increase, exactly? The National Strength and Conditioning Association’s guideline is 2.5 to 5 pounds for upper-body exercises, and 5 to 10 pounds for lower-body exercises. Reminder that this is just a general guide—you can do more or less based on how you specifically feel.

Trying heavier weights is way less intimidating when you have a safety net.

If you’re nervous, ask for a spot. Maybe you already have a gym buddy you workout with regularly that can help pull the barbell up if you get stuck on a bench press. If you don’t, ask one of your gym’s trainers or employees. Most people will politely oblige, and will even appreciate your effort in challenging yourself.

Have a conversation with your spotter before you get into the lift. Tell them how many reps you’re aiming for, and a cue you’ll give them when you want them to jump in and help (my go-to is a simple “now”—since that’s about all you can get out when you’re out of breath).

Some days just don’t feel as strong as others. Maybe you didn’t sleep super well last night, stressed about work, or are at a tough point in your cycle. That’s life. When that happens, you need to respect the cues your body gives you.

If your warmup sets feel unusually heavy, take the hint: this just might not be the day to pick up that heavy weight. It doesn’t mean you’ve regressing, it’s just a bump in the road. Strength, and muscle building, is not a linear process.

Build muscle with the WH+ Build & Burn series

Ultimately, building and maintaining muscle mass is one of the strongest investments you can make in long-term health—especially as you age.

And lifting heavy is one effective way to provide muscle-building stimulus to the body—but it isn’t accessible, comfortable, or safe for everyone all the time. The goal is progressive challenge, and lighter loads can deliver that when you train with intention and effort.

“You do not need to lift heavy to build muscle, but you do need to train with intention,” Reiner says. “The best approach is the one that someone can perform consistently, safely, and with enough effort to challenge the muscle over time.”

Cori Ritchey, C.S.C.S., is the fitness editor at Women's Health, as well as a certified strength and condition coach and group fitness instructor. She’s reported on topics regarding health, nutrition, mental health, fitness, sex, and relationships for several years. You can find more of her work in Men’s Health, HealthCentral, Livestrong, Self, and others.

#4744. RFK Jr.’s Revised Vaccine Schedule May Cause 83% Surge in Hepatitis B Infections

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule have raised alarm among public health experts and researchers.

Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B.

A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ended its recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for the virus. Instead, the federal health agency recommends individual-based clinical decision making.

After reviewing the evidence, the CDC, which is overseen by the HHS, concluded that newborns “face little risk of contracting hepatitis,” which deemed the vaccine, typically administered at birth, unnecessary.

Experts say this shift in public health policy wasn’t based on science, and researchers warn of rising infection rates.

“Hepatitis B immunizations have been proven to protect individuals against a serious and significant disease,” said Graham Tse, MD, pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

“The hepatitis B vaccines have several decades of history and have been proven safe and effective,” Tse said. “There has been no new data or evidence presented or uncovered to support delaying the newborn dose of hepatitis B.”

Here’s what parents should know about making informed decisions with their child’s healthcare team.

A U.S. modeling study published in Annals of Internal Medicine on October 20 projected that delaying the first vaccine dose until 2 months could increase chronic hepatitis B infections among infants by 19% under one scenario.

With shared decision making and lower vaccine uptake, projected increases ranged from 83% to 225%, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination.

The researchers also estimated that up to 1.8 million young adults could remain susceptible to hepatitis B by age 20 under shared decision making, compared with 232,000 under universal birth dosing.

Another study published in JAMA Pediatrics in late April projected hundreds of additional chronic infections annually if the hepatitis B birth dose were delayed or omitted.

However, these figures are model-based projections, rather than verified outcomes. Actual results will depend on vaccination rates and other factors.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) adopted a recommendation shifting away from universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

Under the new approach, parents and healthcare professionals can decide together whether to give the first dose at birth or defer it until the baby is 2 months old.

The change followed an 8 to 3 vote by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), marking a departure from longstanding U.S. guidance.

However, infants born to mothers who test positive for hepatitis B or whose infection status is unknown should still receive the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth, according to the updated guidelines.

Hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver.

Although some infections resolve, newborns and infants face a higher risk of developing lifelong hepatitis B infection compared with adults.

Up to 90% of infants infected during their first year develop chronic hepatitis B.

“We have actual world evidence that vaccinating newborns for hepatitis B prevents hepatitis B infections later in life and the serious complications of that disease,” Tse said.

Over time, chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer.

“The danger of delaying the newborn hepatitis B shot is that individuals do not get vaccinated and thereby do not have protection against hepatitis B,” Tse said.

Early vaccination helps protect young infants before potential exposure occurs, including situations in which maternal screening misses an infection.

“Newborns can be infected with hepatitis B from a mother who is not aware they have a hepatitis B infection or from exposure later in life,” Tse said.

“The risk is developing a hepatitis B infection, which can potentially lead to liver cancer, fulminant hepatitis, or severe end-stage liver disease.”

In contrast to the CDC, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) still recommends a universal hepatitis B vaccine dose within 24 hours of birth, followed by additional doses during infancy.

The leading pediatric medical organization has raised concerns about the potential consequences of reduced vaccination rates.

The hepatitis B vaccine has decades of safety and effectiveness data.

Tse said the AAP’s vaccine schedule and recommendations are based on decades of study, use, and expert input, and provide the best protection against vaccine-preventable diseases.

Parents who have questions about potential side effects, timing, or their baby’s individual risk should discuss them with a qualified healthcare professional.

“Parents are confused, given the recommendations from CDC, HHS, and Kennedy differ from established and respected groups such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Disease Society of America, and several states,” Tse said.

“Parents desire to keep their children safe, and having differing opinions and confusion will lead to reduced vaccination rates as parents experience doubt as to whom to listen to or believe.”

While the updated CDC policy offers more flexibility for some families, lower vaccination uptake could lead to an increase in chronic hepatitis B infections.

Ask your pediatrician about the benefits of vaccination against hepatitis B at birth, the risks of delaying the first dose, and the recommended schedule for completing the series.

You can also ask how maternal screening results affect your baby’s protection.

An informed conversation with your healthcare professional can help you weigh the evidence and choose a vaccination plan for your baby.

“I see no argument whatsoever for changing the established vaccination schedule for hepatitis B,” Tse said.

“There have been no new studies, no data, nor evidence to justify Kennedy’s proposed changes to the childhood immunization schedule. Delaying vaccinations or skipping vaccinations puts your child at risk for serious and significant diseases, which are all preventable,” Tse said.

#4742. The Gift That Keeps on Giving

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

I was running out to grab a cup of coffee and asked my co-worker if I could grab one for her. No biggie, just a common courtesy. I literally didn’t even go out of my way. But when I returned, she couldn't have been more grateful. Sometimes when we do small, simple things, we realize later how much they meant to others.

It could be something like a thoughtful message or a quick check-in where we take a few minutes to listen.

The thing is, we often underestimate the impact of these simple gestures. We are all so busy these days, caught up in daily responsibilities and checking all the boxes to complete everything on our list, that we tend to forget how much we can effortlessly offer to others.

Of course, in this fast-paced world, we are always striving for more from life. And, at the same time, it's important to pause and recognize what we have and how it can be shared with those around us.

Just take a moment to think about some of the people who make a difference in your life. Perhaps it was that friend who checked in on you during a difficult time or a supervisor who encouraged you. They may not have given their generosity much thought, but I bet you remember how it made you feel, right?

Let me share with you a research study that supports this idea. A 2023 study in the Journal of Experimental Psychology found that people frequently underestimate how positive acts of kindness impact others. In one study, participants who gave strangers hot chocolate thought the recipients would be happy, but in reality, the recipients were incredibly grateful for the gesture.

Generativity, a concept developed by psychologist Erik Erikson, describes how a person wants to contribute to the lives of others and make a difference for future generations. This is evidenced in the things that we do, like mentoring others, supporting a friend or family member, or sharing lessons.

It’s important to mention that the research demonstrates a strong connection between helping people and well-being. In 2020, Psychological Bulletin published a meta-analysis of more than 200 studies and found a consistent relationship between helping people and positive well-being.

It’s important to mention that giving to others doesn't mean we are neglecting our needs. It just means that we are also helping one another build relationships. And the research also shows that a sense of connection really matters.

Sadly, we are often so busy managing all that we have to do that we don't think about how we can support others.

Which of these options could you incorporate into your schedule this week? (Choose just one.) You will both benefit if you reach out, offer a little encouragement, listen, or just let someone know they are on your mind. The point is that it doesn't have to be this big grand gesture. Small acts of kindness go a long way.

Life's most meaningful moments happen with people who took the time to listen, remember, or encourage, or helped us feel less alone. Don’t wait for more time or money, or until you've figured everything out, before you try to make a difference. Just start with where you are.

Take a moment and think about one small act of kindness that was bestowed upon you. How can you do the same for others?

Erikson, E. H. (1950). Childhood and society. W. W. Norton.

Holt-Lunstad, J., Smith, T. B., & Layton, J. B. (2010). Social relationships and mortality risk: A meta-analytic review. PLoS Medicine, 7(7), e1000316. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316

Hui, B. P. H., Ng, J. C. K., Berzaghi, E., Cunningham-Amos, L. A., & Kogan, A. (2020). Rewards of kindness? A meta-analysis of the link between prosociality and well-being. Psychological Bulletin, 146(12), 1084–1116. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000298

Kumar, A., & Epley, N. (2023). A little good goes an unexpectedly long way: Underestimating the positive impact of kindness on recipients. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 152(1), 236–252. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0001271
